claims.text: The starting material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
The starting alloy retains an fcc matrix.
The starting alloy exhibits high strength and fatigue performance.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by synergistic interactions among Al, Cr, and Ti that control selective oxidation.
In oxygen-rich environments, Al, Cr, and Ti preferentially oxidize.
Oxidizing exposure produces a coherent, adherent, multilayered protective scale rich in Al and Cr oxides.
The protective oxide scale limits further oxidation and preserves the underlying fcc matrix.
Under reducing conditions, limited oxygen availability produces a less uniform, porous, and non-protective oxide scale.
The non-protective scale formed under reducing conditions accelerates structural degradation.
Oxide-scale composition, thickness, uniformity, and adhesion are the structural mediators linking gas atmosphere to degradation.
Oxidizing exposure will result in slower degradation kinetics than reducing exposure.
The fcc matrix will remain largely intact during the initial stage of reducing exposure despite enhanced degradation.
The controlled comparison should vary oxidizing versus reducing gas atmosphere while holding alloy composition and other processing parameters constant.
The proposed exposure boundary is 750–900°C for approximately 3–6 hours.
Representative oxidizing atmospheres are air or 21% O2 in N2, while representative reducing atmospheres are H2-rich or low-oxygen-partial-pressure mixtures.
Synergistic alloying effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and other elements have improved oxidation resistance or oxidation kinetics in Nb-silicide-based alloys.
Prior multicomponent Nb-silicide research does not clearly isolate which elemental synergies are responsible for improved oxidation resistance.
The quantitative differences in scale thickness, phase composition, and degradation kinetics between the two atmospheres are not established.
The effects of Co, Fe, and Ni on oxide-scale evolution remain unresolved.
A lack of significant atmosphere-dependent differences in scale properties or degradation kinetics would falsify the proposed selective-oxidation mechanism.
